title: Composite fermions in the $ν=3$ fractional quantum spin Hall effect
abstract: Well-understood fractional quantum Hall states in GaAs and graphene can be described in terms of weakly interacting composite fermions. It is natural to expect that the same unifying principle applies to the putative fractional quantum spin Hall effect in MoTe$_2$. Since the quantum spin Hall effect involves two spin components, two types of composite fermions must be present. We classify all two-component composite-fermion states at the filling factor $ν=3$. The classification includes the three classes of states, which were introduced from different physical perspectives in Refs. Sodemann Villadiego, Phys. Rev. B 110, 045114 (2024), Jian et al., Phys. Rev. X 15, 021063 (2025), and May-Mann et al., Phys. Rev. B 111, L201111, (2025), as well as two new classes of states. A majority of the composite-fermion states break the time-reversal symmetry. We review quasiparticle charges, statistics, and edge theories for each possible state. We also address a way of identifying the experimentally relevant state or states. This can be accomplished by combining three probes. First, the shot noise technique provides information about fractional charges. Second, thermal conductance helps count edge modes. The third probe is based on a new idea and involves transport between two quantum point contacts along a single edge. We find that the current from one contact to the other depends on the shape of the edge channel, which can be controlled with a side gate. The probe reveals the emergent symmetry group of the low-energy edge theory.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical framework to classify the complex composite fermion states expected in the fractional quantum spin Hall effect at $\nu=3$. It extends established FQHE concepts to two-spin systems and proposes a rigorous experimental protocol combining shot noise, thermal conductance, and edge tunneling to definitively identify the underlying topological order.
main_problem: To classify and understand the composite fermion (CF) states in the putative fractional quantum spin Hall effect (FQSHE) at filling factor $\nu=3$, and to propose experimental methods to identify the relevant state.
main_result: The paper classifies two-component CF states into several groups (SV, JCX, MSD) and proposes a combination of three experimental probes—shot noise, thermal conductance, and edge tunneling—to uniquely identify the true topological state.
method: The analysis uses the composite fermion picture, extending it to two spin components, and derives theoretical constraints on edge physics using effective Lagrangians and scaling dimensions.
model_or_system: The system is the FQSHE in $\text{MoTe}_2$, modeled using composite fermions that account for two spin components. The theory builds upon established FQHE descriptions by incorporating spin-related degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Fractional quasiparticle charges ($e/2$ or $e/4$), chiral central charge (from thermal conductance), and the emergent symmetry group revealed by edge tunneling.
important_parameters: Filling factor $\nu=3$; the flux quanta parameters ($m, s_1, s_2$); and the scaling dimension $\Delta$ for tunneling operators.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the applicability of the composite fermion picture to the two-component spin system, and that the three proposed experimental probes are sufficient for full characterization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a device setup involving two Quantum Point Contacts (QPCs) connecting the $\nu=3$ edge to other interfaces, relevant for the proposed tunneling measurement.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the CF classification at $\nu=3$, then developing the edge theory using particle-hole transformations and effective Lagrangians, and finally detailing the necessary experimental diagnostics using noise, thermal transport, and tunneling measurements.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed theoretical framework for characterizing topological phases in multi-component systems, which is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in novel 2D materials.
